title: An AI math breakthrough sparks calls for new guardrails
body: “It’s a beautiful piece of mathematics that has been discovered,” says Melanie Matchett Wood of Harvard University, who contributed remarks to an accompanying paper in which outside experts reviewed the AI’s result. The discovery bolsters hopes that AI can contribute to scientific understanding. [...] Mathematician Thomas Bloom of the University of Manchester in England had a similar reaction. He noted in the paper from outside experts on the achievement that it would have been “truly incredible” if the AI had managed to prove the conjecture, as that kind of solution would require creative insight. [...] Researchers at OpenAI gave an AI model Erdős’ conjecture and walked away. When they returned, they discovered a breakthrough: The model had disproved the conjecture in a mathematical proof posted May 20 on OpenAI.com.

title: AI is getting better at hacking power, water systems
body:
The world's most advanced AI models are suddenly capable of blueprinting cyberattacks on critical services like power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research.

Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are running out of time. Top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks, new research from cybersecurity company Frenos shows, and it's only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute. [...] "AI doesn't have the problem with patience," Thomas said. "It doesn't need to eat. It doesn't need to sleep, and it doesn't need to use the restroom."
   Paul Shaver, head of operational technology at cybersecurity firm Armadin, added that AI agents can already conduct reconnaissance and analyze large volumes of data without necessarily triggering security alerts. [...] Threat level:Once attackers gain access to an industrial network, AI could help them quietly map out systems and identify weaknesses without the same time constraints facing human hackers, Frenos co-founder and CTO Harry Thomas said.

title: Microsoft introduces newest in-house AI chip — Maia 200 is faster than other bespoke Nvidia competitors, built on TSMC 3nm with 216GB of HBM3e | Tom's Hardware
body: Microsoft has introduced its newest AI accelerator, the Microsoft Azure Maia 200. The new in-house AI chip is the next generation of Microsoft's Maia GPU line, a server chip designed for inferencing AI models with ludicrous speeds and feeds to outperform the custom offerings from hyperscaler competitors Amazon and Google. [...] Maia 200, originally codenamed Braga, made waves for its heavily delayed development and release. The chip was intended for 2025 release and deployment, maybe even beating B300 out of the gates, but this was not meant to be. Microsoft's next hardware release isn't certain, but it will likely be fabricated on Intel Foundry's 18A process, per reports in October. [...] Maia 200 has already been deployed in Microsoft's US Central Azure data center, with future deployments announced for US West 3 in Phoenix, AZ, and more to come as Microsoft receives more chips. The chip will be part of Microsoft's heterogeneous deployment, operating in tandem with other different AI accelerators as well.

title: Elon Musk reveals roadmap with nine-month cadence for new AI processor releases, beating Nvidia and AMD's yearly cadence — Musk plans to have the highest-volume chips in the world | Tom's Hardware
body: Nvidia tends to release its AI GPUs at an annual cadence, which keeps the company ahead of all rivals. AMD has invested a lot to keep up, so it also launches new AI accelerators on a yearly rhythm. Apparently, Elon Musk wants Tesla to progress even faster and release new AI processors every nine months to perhaps eventually catch up with AMD and then market leader Nvidia. There seems to be caveat with Musk's plans, but he seems to be looking forward a solution. [...] A 9-month design cycle is realistic only if AI6, AI7, AI8, and AI9 are incremental, platform-based iterations, not clean-sheet designs. That means reusing the same core architecture, programming model, memory hierarchy, safety framework, and most IP, with changes limited to scaling compute, tuning SRAM, modest dataflow tweaks, or a planned node retarget. Any attempt to introduce something that goes beyond compute, such as a new memory type, compiler model, coherency scheme, or safety [...] Elon Musk's Tesla is not as prompt as AMD and Nvidia when it comes to releasing new hardware. There is an explanation for this: the company's processors are primarily meant for cars, which require redundancy and safety certifications. While redundancy is common for large high-performance AI processors that tend to be the maximum size possible (the reticle limit of an EUV lithography system), the safety required for cars is a whole different level.
